items.title: Figure 1 caption: Identify an example, different from lifting a barbell, in which a force does work on an object, and state the directions of the force and of the motion.

body.html: Any situation in which a force acts on an object that moves; name the force and motion directions.
Work is done whenever a force has a component along the object's displacement ( 𝑊= 𝐹𝑑cos𝜃).
Think of a tugboat pulling a barge. The rope force points forward and the barge moves forward, so 𝜃= 0° and cos𝜃= + 1.

answer.html: Example: a tugboat's rope pulling a barge along a channel, or a cyclist's leg pushing a pedal downward as it moves down. In each, the force and the motion point (at least partly) in the same direction.

check.html: If the force were perpendicular to the motion (a waiter carrying a tray level), no work would be done.

items.title: Get It? (Work at an angle): A force of 8.0 N acts at 35° to the direction of motion of a cart that moves 2.5 m. How much work does the force do?

body.html: Only the component of the force along the displacement does work: 𝑊= 𝐹𝑑cos𝜃.

check.html: Less than 𝐹𝑑= 20 J, the value for a force straight along the motion.

items.title: Figure 3 caption: Two people push opposite sides of a heavy cart. You push with 60 N and your friend pushes with a larger force of 75 N, and the cart moves 2.0 m. Describe the total work on the cart.

body.html: 𝐹<sub>you</sub> = 60 N, 𝐹<sub>friend</sub> = 75 N, 𝑑= 2.0 m; find 𝑊<sub>total</sub>.

Total work is the sum of the work by each force. The net force, and so the motion, points in the direction of the larger push. Gravity and the normal force are perpendicular to the motion and do zero work.
The friend's force is along the displacement (𝜃= 0°) and yours is opposite it (𝜃= 180°).

answer.html: The total work is positive, 𝑊= (𝐹<sub>friend</sub> −𝐹<sub>you</sub>)𝑑= + 3.0 × 10<sup>1</sup> J. The friend does positive work, you do negative work, and the cart gains kinetic energy moving toward you.

check.html: Same as net force (15 N) times 𝑑: 15 × 2.0 = 30 J.

items.title: Get It? A dog pulls a wagon forward along a path while its owner holds back on a rope tied to the wagon. Why does the dog do positive work on the wagon and the owner negative work?

body.html: The sign of work comes from cos𝜃, the angle between the force and the displacement.

answer.html: The dog's force points in the direction the wagon moves (𝜃= 0°, cos𝜃= + 1), so the dog transfers energy to the wagon (positive work). The owner's force points opposite the motion ( 𝜃= 180°, cos𝜃= −1), so the owner removes energy from the wagon (negative work).

items.title: Get It? Describe a scenario, different from lifting a bag onto a shelf, in which you do work on a system, and calculate how much work you do. (Use a 4.2-kg watering can raised 1.3 m at constant speed.)

body.html: 𝑚= 4.2 kg, ℎ= 1.3 m; find the work done on the can.
Lifting at constant speed requires an upward force equal to the weight, and 𝑊= 𝐹𝑑.
Weight: 𝑚𝑔= (4.2 kg)(9.80 m/s<sup>2</sup>) = 41.2 N.

answer.html: Example: lifting a 4.2-kg watering can 1.3 m onto a counter at constant speed does about 54 J of work on it. (Any reasonable scenario with the correct 𝑊= 𝐹𝑑cos𝜃 is acceptable.)

check.html: A 41-N force over about 1 m is a few tens of joules, reasonable.

items.title: Practice Problems after Example Problem 1 (work by a constant force) Problem 1a. A student pulls a lab cart with a 6.20-N force along its track for 0.220 m. The force is then tripled to 18.6 N over the same distance. How is the work affected?

body.html: 𝐹<sub>1</sub> = 6.20 N, 𝐹<sub>2</sub> = 18.6 N, 𝑑= 0.220 m; compare 𝑊.
𝑊= 𝐹𝑑 (force along the motion), so 𝑊 is directly proportional to 𝐹 when 𝑑 is fixed.

answer.html: The work triples, from 1.36 J to 4.09 J.

check.html: Tripling 𝐹 with 𝑑 fixed must triple 𝑊 (1.36 × 3 = 4.09).

items.title: 1b. The 18.6-N force now acts over only one-third of the distance (0.0733 m). What is the work?

body.html: Same equation, 𝑊= 𝐹𝑑; the force tripled but the distance shrank to a third.

answer.html: 𝑊= 1.36 J, the same as the first case: tripling the force while cutting the distance to a third leaves the work unchanged.

items.title: 2a. Two movers push a piano on a level floor with a combined force of 640 N for 18 m. How much work do they do?

body.html: 𝐹= 640 N, 𝑑= 18 m, 𝜃= 0°; find 𝑊.
Force along the motion, so 𝑊= 𝐹𝑑.

check.html: A large force over a large distance gives tens of kilojoules, reasonable.

items.title: 2b. A third mover joins and the combined force triples (to 1920 N) over the same distance. What is the work?

answer.html: 𝑊= 3.5 × 10<sup>4</sup> J (three times the original work)

items.title: 3a. A hiker lifts a 5.8-kg pack 11.5 m up a cliff face at a steady pace over 20.0 min. How much work is done on the pack?

body.html: 𝑚= 5.8 kg, ℎ= 11.5 m, 𝑔= 9.80 m/s<sup>2</sup>; find the work done on the pack.
To raise the pack at a steady pace the hiker must exert an upward force equal to its weight, 𝐹= 𝑚𝑔, through the vertical distance. (The 20.0 min is not needed for work.)

items.title: 3b. The hiker weighs 585 N. How much work does she do lifting both herself and the pack up the 11.5 m?

body.html: Her weight is already a force (585 N). Work on herself: (585 N)(11.5 m) = 6728 J. Add the pack's 654 J:

items.title: 4 (Challenge). Dmitri pushes a 4.5-kg crate 6.0 m across a floor with a 16-N horizontal force, then lifts it 1.5 m onto a shelf. How much total work does Dmitri do on the crate?

body.html: Total work is the sum of the work in each stage. Pushing: force along the motion. Lifting: force equals the weight, 𝑚𝑔, through the height.

check.html: The weight does no work while the crate slides horizontally; each stage is added, not canceled.

items.title: Practice Problems after Example Problem 2 (force at an angle) Problem 1. A student pulls a sled 42.0 m along level snow with a rope that makes a 35.0° angle with the ground, using 185 N of force. How much work does the student do?

body.html: Only the part of the rope force along the ground does work: 𝑊= 𝐹𝑑cos𝜃.

check.html: Smaller than 𝐹𝑑= 7.77 × 10<sup>3</sup> J, the maximum, because only part of the force points along the snow.

items.title: 2. Two workers hoist a crate 8.0 m straight up using ropes that each make a 20° angle with the vertical. Each rope pulls with 310 N. How much work do the two ropes do together?

body.html: The crate moves vertically, so each rope's force makes 20° with the displacement. Only the vertical component, 𝐹cos20°, does work.

items.title: 3a. A hiker carries a 142-N daypack up a trail section that rises 3.60 m vertically while covering 5.20 m horizontally. How much work does the hiker do on the pack?

body.html: Carrying the pack at steady speed, the hiker's force is upward and equals the weight (142 N). Only the vertical part of the displacement (3.60 m) is along this force; the 5.20 m horizontal displacement is perpendicular to it and contributes no work.

items.title: 3b. The hiker carries the pack back down the same section of trail. How much work does the hiker do on the pack?

body.html: The force is still upward (142 N) but the vertical displacement is now downward, so 𝜃= 180°.

answer.html: 𝑊= −5.11 × 10<sup>2</sup> J (negative work: energy leaves the pack)

items.title: 4. A rope at 38.0° above the horizontal drags a log 22.0 m along the ground with a 410-N force. How much work does the rope do?

body.html: 𝑊= 𝐹𝑑cos𝜃 with 𝜃= 38.0° between the rope and the motion.

check.html: Less than 𝐹𝑑= 9.02 × 10<sup>3</sup> J, which is the maximum.

items.title: 5a (Challenge). A cyclist pushes an 11.0-kg bicycle 180 m up a 15° hill, exerting 38 N parallel to the road. How much work does the cyclist do on the bicycle?

body.html: The pushing force is parallel to the road and the displacement is along the road, so 𝜃= 0°.

items.title: 5b. How much work does gravity do on the bicycle during the climb?

body.html: Gravity (weight 𝑚𝑔) points straight down. The bike rises a vertical height ℎ= 𝑑sin15° , so the angle between gravity and displacement is 90° + 15° = 105°. Equivalent: 𝑊<sub>𝑔</sub>= −𝑚𝑔ℎ.
𝑊<sub>𝑔</sub>= −𝑚𝑔𝑑sin𝜃= −(11.0 kg)(9.80 m/s<sup>2</sup>)(180 m)sin15° = −5.02 × 10<sup>3</sup> J

check.html: Negative, because gravity opposes the climb. The net work is +1.8 × 10<sup>3</sup> J, so (ignoring friction) the bike would also gain kinetic energy.

items.title: Figure 8 caption: Identify two other events, different from lifting a box, in which work causes a change in energy.

answer.html: (1) Hitting a baseball with a bat: the bat does positive work, increasing the ball's kinetic energy. (2) A runner dragging a foot on a track to stop: friction does negative work, decreasing the runner's kinetic energy. (Drawing back a bowstring or stretching a rubber band also qualify: work changes elastic potential energy.)

body.html: Work-energy theorem: 𝑊= 𝛥𝐾𝐸=<sup> </sup><sup>12</sup>𝑚(𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub>

items.title: 2. A 41.0-kg child on roller skates coasts at 3.6 m/s and stops after 18.0 m. Find the initial kinetic energy, the energy friction transforms, and the work the child must do to speed back up to 3.6 m/s.

body.html: 𝐾𝐸=<sup> </sup><sup>12</sup>𝑚𝑣<sup>2</sup>. As the child stops, friction does negative work equal to −𝐾𝐸<sub>𝑖</sub>, converting all of it to other forms (thermal). To regain the speed the child must supply the same energy.

answer.html: Initial 𝐾𝐸= 2.7 × 10<sup>2</sup> J; friction transforms all of it, 2.7 × 10<sup>2</sup> J, into other forms (mainly thermal); the child must do 𝑊= 2.7 × 10<sup>2</sup> J to speed back up to 3.6 m/s.

check.html: The 18.0 m is not needed for the energy values (it would give the friction force, about 14.8 N).

items.title: 3. A 1150.0-kg van speeds up from 18.0 m/s to 27.0 m/s. Find its initial and final kinetic energy and the net work done on it.

body.html: 𝐾𝐸=<sup> </sup><sup>12</sup>𝑚𝑣<sup>2</sup> and 𝑊= 𝐾𝐸<sub>𝑓</sub>−𝐾𝐸<sub>𝑖</sub>.
𝐾𝐸<sub>𝑖</sub>= 12

answer.html: 𝐾𝐸<sub>𝑖</sub>= 1.86 × 10<sup>5</sup> J, 𝐾𝐸<sub>𝑓</sub>= 4.19 × 10<sup>5</sup> J, 𝑊= 2.33 × 10<sup>5</sup> J

check.html: Speed grows by a factor 1.5, so 𝐾𝐸 grows by 1.5<sup>2</sup> = 2.25 (4.19 / 1.86 = 2.25).

items.title: 4 (Challenge). An asteroid of mass 3.20 × 1010 kg strikes Earth at 18.0 km/s. Find its kinetic energy, the work Earth does stopping it, and how it compares with a 2.1 × 1017 J bomb.

body.html: 𝐾𝐸=<sub> </sub><sub>12</sub>𝑚𝑣<sup>2</sup> with 𝑣= 1.80 × 10<sup>4</sup> m/s. Earth stops the asteroid, so Earth does negative work equal to −𝐾𝐸; compare magnitudes with 2.1 × 10<sup>17</sup> J.

answer.html: 𝐾𝐸= 5.18 × 10<sup>18</sup> J. Earth does −5.18 × 10<sup>18</sup> J of work stopping it, about 25 times the energy of the bomb.

items.title: Practice Problems after Example Problem 3 (power) Problem 1. A winch lifts an 840-N crate 12.0 m at constant velocity in 9.00 s. What power does the winch deliver?

body.html: Constant velocity means the cable force equals the weight, 𝐹= 840 N. 𝑃= 𝑊/ 𝑡= 𝐹𝑑/ 𝑡.

items.title: 2a. A lawn mower is pushed 75.0 m at constant speed in 40.0 s with a 90.0-N force. What power does the person deliver?

body.html: 𝑃= 𝑊/ 𝑡= 𝐹𝑑/ 𝑡.

items.title: 2b. The person now covers the same 75.0 m 1.5 times as fast. What power is needed?

body.html: Same force and distance means the same work, but in less time: 𝑡= 40.0 / 1.5 = 26.7 s. Equivalently, 𝑃= 𝐹𝑣 and 𝑣 is 1.5 times larger.

items.title: 3. An irrigation pump lifts 120 L of water per minute from a well 28 m deep. What power must the pump supply? (1 L of water has a mass of 1 kg.)

body.html: In 𝑡= 60 s: 𝑚= 120 kg, ℎ= 28 m.
The pump must supply a force equal to the weight of the water.

items.title: 4. A crane motor develops 48 kW lifting a load 22.0 m in 28 s. What force does the cable exert on the load?

body.html: 𝑃= 𝐹𝑑/ 𝑡, so 𝐹= 𝑃𝑡/ 𝑑.

check.html: Equivalent to lifting about 6200 kg, a heavy construction load, plausible.

items.title: 5 (Challenge). A winch with a pulling force of 4.2 × 103 N and a power of 0.45 kW drags a boat trailer 9.0 m. How long does it take?

body.html: Work needed is 𝐹𝑑; the winch supplies it at rate 𝑃, so 𝑡= 𝐹𝑑/ 𝑃.

items.title: Lesson 1 Check Your Progress Problem 1. Use the work-energy theorem to describe lifting a backpack from the floor to a desk, starting and ending at rest.

body.html: 𝑊= 𝛥𝐸. The backpack starts and ends at rest, so its kinetic energy does not change; the energy that changes is gravitational potential energy.

answer.html: You do positive work on the backpack (force upward, displacement upward), 𝑊= 𝑚𝑔ℎ, which equals the increase in the backpack-Earth system's gravitational potential energy, 𝛥𝐺𝑃𝐸= 𝑚𝑔ℎ. Gravity does equal negative work, so the net work on the backpack is zero (no change in kinetic energy).

items.title: 2. Net work triples the kinetic energy of a cart. By what factor does its speed increase? What would be needed to triple the speed?

body.html: 𝐾𝐸=<sup> </sup><sup>12</sup>𝑚𝑣<sup>2</sup>, so 𝑣= √2𝐾𝐸/ 𝑚.
If 𝐾𝐸<sub>𝑓</sub>= 3𝐾𝐸<sub>𝑖</sub> then 𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub>

answer.html: The speed increases by a factor of √3 ≈1.73, not 3. (To triple the speed you must increase the kinetic energy by a factor of 9.)

items.title: 3. Amara slides a 35-kg crate 6.0 m across a floor with a horizontal 55-N force. How much work does she do on the crate?

body.html: Force along the motion, so 𝑊= 𝐹𝑑.

answer.html: 𝑊= 3.3 × 10<sup>2</sup> J (the mass is not needed)

items.title: 4. A trolley is pushed 8.0 m along a track. The force rises linearly from 25.0 N at the start to 175.0 N at the end. Draw the force-displacement graph and find the work done.

body.html: Work is the area under the force-displacement graph. The graph is a trapezoid (or: average force times distance).

answer.html: 𝑊= 8.0 × 10<sup>2</sup> J (graph: a straight line sloping up from 25 N at 0 m to 175 N at 8.0 m; the shaded area beneath it is the work)

check.html: Between the smallest possible (25 × 8 = 200 J) and largest possible (175 × 8 = 1400 J) values, right at the midpoint.

items.title: 5. A mover pushes a 142-kg washing machine at constant speed 6.50 m up a frictionless 18° ramp. How much work does the mover do?

body.html: Constant speed means the push parallel to the ramp balances the component of weight along the ramp: 𝐹= 𝑚𝑔sin𝜃. The work equals the gain in potential energy.
𝑊= 𝐹𝑑= 𝑚𝑔sin𝜃𝑑= (142 kg)(9.80 m/s<sup>2</sup>)sin18°(6.50 m) = 2.80 × 10<sup>3</sup> J

check.html: Equals 𝑚𝑔ℎ with ℎ= 6.50sin18° = 2.01 m.

items.title: 6. How much work does gravity do on a 0.250-kg apple falling 3.4 m from a branch?

body.html: The force of gravity (𝑚𝑔) and the displacement point the same way, so 𝑊<sub>𝑔</sub>= 𝑚𝑔ℎ.

answer.html: 𝑊<sub>𝑔</sub>= 8.3 J (positive, because gravity and the motion point the same way)

items.title: 7. Does the work you do carrying a box up a flight of stairs depend on whether you walk or run? Does the power?

body.html: 𝑊= 𝐹𝑑 depends only on the force and distance; 𝑃= 𝑊/ 𝑡 depends on the time.

answer.html: The work does not depend on your pace (same force, same height). The power does: running does the same work in less time, so the power is larger.

items.title: 8. A freight lift raises 2.4 × 103 kg a distance of 18.0 m in 15.0 s. What power does it develop?

body.html: Assuming steady speed, the lifting force equals the weight, 𝐹= 𝑚𝑔.

items.title: 9. A winch raises a crate 3.5 m and does 12 kJ of work on it. What is the crate's mass?

body.html: 𝑊= 𝑚𝑔ℎ, so 𝑚= 𝑊/ (𝑔ℎ).

items.title: 10. You carry a box up a flight of stairs and then 30 m along a hallway; a friend carries an identical box 30 m along the hallway first and then up the same stairs. Compare the work each of you does against gravity.

body.html: Lifting force equals the weight (vertical). Only vertical displacement is along that force. Horizontal carrying (force vertical, motion horizontal) does zero work.

answer.html: Both of you do the same work, 𝑊= 𝑚𝑔ℎ, where ℎ is the height of the stairs. The order and the path do not matter because the horizontal part of the trip involves no work against gravity.

items.title: 11. A crate sliding across a floor is acted on by a rope, by friction, and by a person's push. How do you find the change in the crate's energy?

body.html: Work-energy theorem with several forces.

answer.html: Calculate the work done by each of the three forces separately, 𝑊= 𝐹𝑑cos𝜃 (with the correct sign for each; friction does negative work), and add them: 𝑊<sub>net</sub> = 𝑊<sub>rope</sub> + 𝑊<sub>friction</sub> + 𝑊<sub>push</sub>. This sum equals the change in the crate's kinetic energy, 𝛥𝐾𝐸= 𝑊<sub>net</sub>.

items.title: Figure 1 caption: Identify another example of when a force does work on an object.

body.html: Work is done whenever a force has a component along the object's displacement ( 𝑊= 𝐹𝑑cos𝜃).

answer.html: Examples: a weightlifter's hands lifting a barbell upward; a horse pulling a plow along the field; a person pushing a shopping cart. In each, the force and the motion point (at least partly) in the same direction.

items.title: Get It? (Work at an angle): force of 3 N at 45° to the motion for 1 m

body.html: 𝐹= 3 N, 𝜃= 45°, 𝑑= 1 m; find 𝑊.
Only the component of the force along the displacement does work: 𝑊= 𝐹𝑑cos𝜃.

answer.html: 𝑊≈2 J (2.1 J before rounding to the 1 significant figure of the 3 N)

check.html: Less than the 3 J you would do with a force straight along the motion, as expected.

items.title: Figure 3 caption: Describe the total work on the box if your friend exerted a greater force than you did.

body.html: Total work is the sum of the work by each force: 𝑊<sub>total</sub> = 𝐹<sub>you</sub>𝑑−𝐹<sub>friend</sub>𝑑 when the displacement is in the direction of the net force. Gravity and the normal force are perpendicular to the motion and do zero work.

If the friend pushes harder, the net force (and therefore the box's displacement) points in the friend's direction. Now the friend's force is along the displacement (positive work, +𝐹<sub>friend</sub>𝑑) and your force is opposite it (negative work, −𝐹<sub>you</sub>𝑑).

answer.html: The total work, 𝑊= (𝐹<sub>friend</sub> −𝐹<sub>you</sub>)𝑑, is positive: the friend does positive work and you do negative work, and the box gains kinetic energy moving toward you.

items.title: Get It? Why do you do positive work on the box and your friend negative work?

body.html: The sign of work comes from cos𝜃, the angle between the force and the displacement.

answer.html: Your force points in the same direction the box moves (𝜃= 0°, cos𝜃= + 1), so you transfer energy to the box (positive work). Your friend's force points opposite the motion ( 𝜃= 180°, cos𝜃= −1), so the friend removes energy from the box (negative work).

body.html: The pushing force is parallel to the road and the displacement is along the road, so 𝜃= 0°.

items.title: 5b. Work done by gravity on the bike

body.html: Gravity (weight 𝑚𝑔) points straight down. The bike rises a vertical height ℎ= 𝑑sin25° , so the angle between gravity and displacement is 90° + 25° = 115°. Equivalent: 𝑊<sub>𝑔</sub>= −𝑚𝑔ℎ.
𝑊<sub>𝑔</sub>= −𝑚𝑔𝑑sin𝜃= −(13 kg)(9.80 m/s<sup>2</sup>)(275 m)sin25° = −1.48 × 10<sup>4</sup> J

check.html: Negative, because gravity opposes the climb. (The net work is −7.9 × 10<sup>3</sup> J, so with only a 25-N push the bike could not actually be pushed up at steady speed; the rider's force is too small for this idealized case, but the calculation of each work still holds.)

items.title: Figure 8 caption: Identify two other events in which work causes a change in energy

answer.html: (1) Kicking a stationary soccer ball: the foot does positive work, increasing the ball's kinetic energy. (2) Braking a bicycle: the brake pads do negative work, decreasing the bike's kinetic energy. (Lifting a box or stretching a spring also qualify: work changes potential energy.)

items.title: Lesson 1 Check Your Progress Problem 1. Work-energy theorem for lifting a bowling ball from a rack to your shoulder

body.html: 𝑊= 𝛥𝐸. The ball starts and ends at rest, so its kinetic energy does not change; the energy that changes is gravitational potential energy.

answer.html: You do positive work on the ball (force upward, displacement upward), 𝑊= 𝑚𝑔ℎ, which equals the increase in the ball-Earth system's gravitational potential energy, 𝛥𝐺𝑃𝐸= 𝑚𝑔ℎ. Gravity does equal negative work, so the net work on the ball is zero (no change in kinetic energy).

items.title: 7. Does the work or the power to lift a book depend on how fast you lift it?

body.html: 𝑊= 𝐹𝑑 depends only on the force and distance; 𝑃= 𝑊/ 𝑡 depends on the time.

answer.html: The work does not depend on how fast you raise the book (same force, same height). The power does: lifting it faster does the same work in less time, so the power is larger.

items.title: 10. Box carried up stairs then along the hall, versus along the hall then up the stairs

body.html: Lifting force equals the weight (vertical). Only vertical displacement is along that force. Horizontal carrying (force vertical, motion horizontal) does zero work.

answer.html: Both of you do the same work, 𝑊= 𝑚𝑔ℎ, where ℎ is the height of one floor. The order and the path do not matter because the horizontal part of the trip involves no work against gravity.

items.title: 11. Change in energy when three agents exert forces at once

body.html: Work-energy theorem with several forces.

answer.html: Calculate the work done by each of the three forces separately, 𝑊= 𝐹𝑑cos𝜃 (with the correct sign for each), and add them: 𝑊<sub>net</sub> = 𝑊<sub>1</sub> + 𝑊<sub>2</sub> + 𝑊<sub>3</sub>. This sum equals the change in the system's energy, 𝛥𝐸= 𝑊<sub>net</sub>.
